danish.title: Fjerde bog (1806) — Kapitel 10
paragraphs: Rostovs andel i Dolokhov's duel med Bezukhov blev dysset ned takket være den gamle greves bestræbelser, og i stedet for at blive degraderet til menig, som han havde forventet, blev han udnævnt til adjudant hos generalguvernøren i Moskva. Som følge heraf kunne han ikke tage med resten af familien på landet, men måtte tilbringe hele sommeren i Moskva med sine nye pligter. Dolokhov kom sig, og Rostov knyttede et nært venskab med ham under hans rekonvalescens. Dolokhov lå syg hos sin mor, der elskede ham lidenskabeligt og ømt, og den gamle Marja Ivanovna, som var blevet glad for Rostov på grund af hans venskab med hendes Fedja, talte ofte med ham om sin søn.

»Ja, greve,« plejede hun at sige, »han er for ædel og ren til vores nuværende, fordærvede verden. Ingen sætter pris på dyd nu til dags; det virker som en bebrejdelse mod alle. Sig mig, greve, var det ret og ærligt af Bezukhov? Og Fedja, med sin ædle sjæl, elskede ham og siger den dag i dag aldrig et ondt ord om ham. De optøjer i Petersborg, da de lavede numre med en politimand — gjorde de det ikke sammen? Og hvad skete der? Bezukhov slap fri, mens Fedja måtte bære hele byrden. Tænk, hvad han har måttet gennemgå! Det er rigtigt, han er blevet genindsat, men hvordan kunne de lade være? Jeg tror ikke, der var mange så tapre fædrelandssønner derude som han. Og nu — den her duel! Har de mennesker ingen følelse eller ære? At vide, at han er enebarn, og så udfordre ham og skyde så præcist! Gud ske lov, at Herren forbarmede sig. Og hvad var det hele for? Hvem har ikke sine intriger nu til dags? Ja, var han så jaloux, burde han vel for min skyld have vist det tidligere, men nej — han lader det gå i månedsvis. Og så kalder han ham ud, fordi han regner med, at Fedja ikke slår sig, fordi han skylder ham penge! Hvilken lavhed! Hvilken usselhed! Jeg ved, De forstår Fedja, min kære greve; og det er derfor, jeg er så glad for Dem. Få mennesker forstår ham. Hans sjæl er så ophøjet, så himmelsk!«
Dolokhov selv talte under sin rekonvalescens til Rostov på en måde, man aldrig ville have ventet af ham.

»Jeg ved godt, folk anser mig for et dårligt menneske!« sagde han. »Lad dem! Jeg bryder mig ikke en smule om andre end dem, jeg elsker; men dem, jeg elsker, elsker jeg, så jeg ville give mit liv for dem, og resten kvæler jeg, hvis de stiller sig i vejen. Jeg har en tilbedt, uvurderlig mor og to-tre venner — dig iblandt — og hvad angår resten, bryder jeg mig kun om dem, for så vidt de er til skade eller nytte. Og de fleste er til skade, især kvinderne. Ja, kære ven,« fortsatte han, »jeg har mødt elskende, ædle, højsindede mænd, men en kvinde — grevinde eller kokkepige — der ikke kunne købes, har jeg endnu ikke mødt. Jeg har endnu ikke fundet den guddommelige renhed og hengivenhed, jeg søger hos en kvinde. Fandt jeg en sådan, ville jeg give mit liv for hende! Men de andre!...« og han gjorde en foragtelig håndbevægelse. »Og tro mig, hvis jeg stadig sætter pris på mit liv, er det kun fordi jeg stadig håber at møde et sådant guddommeligt væsen, der kan genskabe, rense og ophøje mig. Men det forstår du ikke.«
»Jo, det forstår jeg udmærket,« svarede Rostov, der var under sin nye vens indflydelse.

Om efteråret vendte familien Rostov tilbage til Moskva. Tidligt på vinteren kom Denisov også tilbage og boede hos dem. Den første halvdel af vinteren 1806, som Nikolaj Rostov tilbragte i Moskva, var en af de lykkeligste og muntreste tider for ham og hele familien. Nikolaj bragte mange unge mænd med hjem til forældrenes hus. Vera var en smuk pige på tyve; Sonja en pige på seksten med al den charme, en udspringende blomst har; Natasja, halvt voksen og halvt barn, var snart barnligt morsom, snart pigeagtigt fortryllende.

På den tid herskede der i Rostovernes hus en forelskelsens atmosfære, som er typisk for hjem, hvor der findes meget unge og meget charmerende piger. Enhver ung mand, der kom i huset — og så disse modtagelige, smilende unge ansigter (smilende sandsynligvis af egen lykke), mærkede den ivrige travlhed omkring sig og hørte de usammenhængende, men venlige udbrud af sang og musik og de unge pigers tilfældige, men venlige plapren, rede til alt og fulde af håb — oplevede den samme følelse: en parathed til at forelske sig og en forventning om lykke, som han delte med Rostov-familiens unge mennesker.

Blandt de unge mænd, Rostov introducerede, var Dolokhov en af de første, og alle i huset kunne lide ham undtagen Natasja. Hun var ved at komme op at skændes med sin bror på grund af ham. Hun fastholdt, at han var et dårligt menneske, at Pierre i duellen med Bezukhov havde ret og Dolokhov uret, og desuden at han var ubehagelig og unaturlig.

»Der er ingenting at forstå,« råbte hun med trodsig selvsikkerhed, »han er ond og hjerteløs. Se nu, jeg kan godt lide din Denisov, selvom han er en levemand og alt muligt — ham kan jeg alligevel godt lide; så du kan se, jeg forstår nok. Jeg ved ikke, hvordan jeg skal sige det ... med den her er alt udregnet, og det kan jeg ikke lide. Men Denisov ...«

»Nå, Denisov er noget helt andet,« svarede Nikolaj og antydede, at selv Denisov var intet sammenlignet med Dolokhov — »du burde forstå, hvilken sjæl der bor i Dolokhov, du skulle se ham med sin mor. Sikke et hjerte!«
»Det ved jeg ikke noget om, men jeg har det skidt i hans selskab. Og ved du, han er blevet forelsket i Sonja?«
»Sikke noget vrøvl ...«
»Det er jeg sikker på; du skal nok se.«

Natasjas forudsigelse gik i opfyldelse. Dolokhov, som normalt ikke brød sig om dameselskab, begyndte at komme ofte i huset, og spørgsmålet om, for hvis skyld han kom (skønt ingen talte om det), blev hurtigt afklaret. Han kom for Sonjas skyld. Og Sonja, selvom hun aldrig ville have vovet at sige det, vidste det og blev skarlagenrød, hver gang Dolokhov dukkede op.

Dolokhov spiste ofte hos familien Rostov, forpassede aldrig en forestilling, de overværede, og kom til Iogels baller for unge mennesker, som Rostoverne altid deltog i. Han var påfaldende opmærksom mod Sonja og så på hende på en måde, der ikke blot gjorde det umuligt for hende at bære hans blik uden at rødme, men selv den gamle grevinde og Natasja rødmede, når de så hans blikke.
Det var tydeligt, at denne mærkelige, stærke mand var under uimodståelig indflydelse af den mørke, yndefulde pige, som elskede en anden.

Rostov bemærkede noget nyt i Dolokhov's forhold til Sonja, men han forklarede ikke over for sig selv, hvad dette nye bestod i. »De er altid forelskede i nogen,« tænkte han om Sonja og Natasja. Men han var ikke lige så afslappet med Sonja og Dolokhov som før og var sjældnere hjemme.

I efteråret 1806 talte alle igen om krigen med Napoleon med endnu større iver end året før. Der blev givet ordre til at udskrive rekrutter — ti mand af hver tusind til den stående hær og desuden ni af hver tusind til militsien. Overalt blev Bonaparte forbandet, og i Moskva var den kommende krig det eneste samtaleemne. For familien Rostov lå hele interessen i disse krigsforanstaltninger i, at Nikolaj ikke ville høre tale om at blive i Moskva, men blot ventede på, at Denisovs orlov efter jul var udløbet, for at vende tilbage til regimentet sammen med ham. Hans forestående afrejse hindrede ham ikke i at more sig, men gav snarere hans glæder en ekstra krydderi. Han tilbragte størstedelen af tiden uden for hjemmet — til middage, selskaber og baller.

english.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: Rostov's involvement in Dolokhov's duel with Bezukhov was smoothed over through the efforts of old Count Rostov, and instead of being demoted to the ranks as he'd expected, Nicholas was appointed adjutant to the governor-general of Moscow. As a result, he couldn't go to the country with the rest of the family and was kept in Moscow all summer by his new duties. Dolokhov recovered, and Rostov grew very close to him during his convalescence. Dolokhov lay ill at his mother's home — she loved him passionately and tenderly — and old Mary Ivanovna, who had taken a liking to Rostov because of his friendship with her Fedya, often talked to him about her son.

"Yes, Count," she would say, "he is too noble and pure-hearted for this depraved world of ours. Nobody values virtue anymore — it seems like a reproach to everyone. Now tell me, Count — was it right, was it honorable, what Bezukhov did? And Fedya, with his noble spirit, loved him and still doesn't say a word against him. Those pranks in Petersburg when they played tricks on a policeman — didn't they do it together? And look! Bezukhov got off without a scratch while Fedya had to shoulder the whole burden. Think what he went through! Yes, he's been reinstated, but how could they not reinstate him? I doubt there were many sons of the fatherland out there as brave as he was. And now this duel! Have these people no sense of decency or honor? Knowing he's an only son, to challenge him and shoot so accurately! Thank God He had mercy on us. And what was it all about? Who doesn't have affairs these days? If he was so jealous — to my mind — he should have said something sooner, instead of letting it go on for months. And then to challenge him, counting on Fedya not fighting because he owed him money! How low! How contemptible! I know you understand Fedya, my dear Count — and believe me, that's why I'm so fond of you. Very few people truly understand him. He has such a noble, heavenly soul!"
Dolokhov himself, during his recovery, spoke to Rostov in a way no one would have expected.

"I know people think I'm a bad man!" he said. "Let them! I don't care about anyone except those I love. But the people I love, I love so fiercely I'd give my life for them — and everyone else I'd crush if they got in my way. I have a wonderful, priceless mother and two or three friends — you among them — and as for the rest, they only matter to me insofar as they're harmful or useful. And most of them are harmful, especially the women. Yes, my friend," he went on, "I've met loving, noble, high-minded men, but I've never yet met a woman — whether countess or kitchen maid — who wasn't mercenary. I haven't found that divine purity and devotion I look for in a woman. If I found someone like that, I'd give my life for her! But these..." and he made a gesture of contempt. "And believe me, if I still value my life, it's only because I still hope to find such a heavenly creature — someone who will transform, purify, and lift me up. But you don't understand that."
"Oh yes, I understand completely," answered Rostov, who was now fully under his new friend's influence.

In the autumn the Rostovs returned to Moscow. Early in the winter Denisov arrived too and stayed with them. The first half of the winter of 1806, which Nicholas Rostov spent in Moscow, was one of the happiest and most carefree times for him and the whole family. Nicholas brought many young men home to his parents' house. Vera was a striking girl of twenty; Sonya was a girl of sixteen with all the charm of a flower just opening; Natasha — half grown-up and half child — was sometimes childishly amusing, sometimes enchantingly girlish.

At that time the Rostov household was filled with the kind of romantic atmosphere typical of homes where there are very young and very charming girls. Every young man who visited — seeing those responsive, smiling young faces (smiling, no doubt, at their own happiness), feeling the eager energy around him, and hearing the bursts of song and music and the lighthearted, open chatter of girls ready for anything and full of hope — felt the same thing: a shared readiness to fall in love and an expectation that happiness was just around the corner.

Among the young men Nicholas brought to the house, one of the first was Dolokhov, whom everyone liked except Natasha. She nearly quarreled with her brother over him. She insisted that he was a bad person, that Pierre had been in the right in the duel and Dolokhov in the wrong, and furthermore that he was disagreeable and fake.

"There's nothing to understand," she declared with stubborn conviction. "He's cruel and heartless. Look — I like your Denisov, even though he's a wild one and all that — I still like him. So you see, I can judge people. But with this one, everything is calculated, and I don't like that. But Denisov..."

"Oh, Denisov is completely different," replied Nicholas, implying that even Denisov was nothing compared to Dolokhov. "You need to understand what kind of soul Dolokhov has — you should see him with his mother. What a heart!"
"Well, I don't know about all that, but I'm uncomfortable around him. And did you know he's fallen in love with Sonya?"
"That's nonsense..."
"I'm sure of it. You'll see."

Natasha's prediction turned out to be right. Dolokhov, who normally didn't seek out women's company, began visiting the house frequently, and the question of whom he was coming to see — though nobody spoke of it openly — was soon answered. He came for Sonya. And Sonya, though she would never have dared say it aloud, knew it and blushed bright red every time Dolokhov appeared.

Dolokhov often dined at the Rostovs', never missed a performance they attended, and went to Iogel's dance parties for young people, which the Rostovs always frequented. He was pointedly attentive to Sonya and looked at her in a way that made not only her blush but even the old countess and Natasha turn red when they noticed his gaze.
It was obvious that this strange, powerful man was under the irresistible spell of the dark, graceful girl who loved someone else.

Rostov noticed something new in Dolokhov's behavior toward Sonya, but he didn't try to figure out what these new dynamics meant. "They're always falling in love with somebody," he thought about Sonya and Natasha. But he wasn't as comfortable around Sonya and Dolokhov as before, and he spent less time at home.

In the autumn of 1806, talk of war with Napoleon had flared up again, even more intensely than the year before. Orders went out to raise recruits — ten men from every thousand for the regular army, plus nine from every thousand for the militia. Bonaparte was denounced everywhere, and in Moscow nothing was talked about but the coming war. For the Rostov family, the real significance of all these war preparations was that Nicholas refused to stay in Moscow and was only waiting for Denisov's leave to end after Christmas so he could return with him to their regiment. His approaching departure didn't stop him from enjoying himself — if anything, it added urgency to his pleasures. He spent most of his time away from home, at dinners, parties, and balls.
